title: Iteration 1, 5, 20
spec: M24 · what the loop carries, and what it quietly loses
intro: One agent, twenty tool calls, one lien total. Nothing breaks. The window just fills, a compaction fires to save it, and the thing it folds away is the record of the state the agent already covered.

provenance.source: a narrated 20-iteration UCC investigation loop; window sizes, budgets, costs and lien counts are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: This walks M24's The Scratchpad and Context Pressure — pin the goal and running state, shape each tool result to its finding, drop the raw dump, checkpoint.

steps.title: Iteration 1 — the board is empty and everything fits
narrative: The goal: total active lien exposure for ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION and its affiliates, every state it operates in. Twenty tool calls — twelve state searches and eight affiliate resolutions — one per iteration.

The loop has a fixed floor of 2,360 tokens: system rules, tool definitions and the goal line. Iteration 1 queries Florida, gets back a 2,700-token dump of filing records, extracts FL: 5 active liens, and appends the whole dump to the history. Window: 5,060 tokens against a 40,000-token working budget.
This is the detective's case board on day one, with one photo pinned to it. Everything the agent knows is legible from six inches away, which is exactly why nobody thinks about the board's size yet.
steps.youDo: Print len(tokenize(window)) at the top of every iteration of your own loop. The number is the whole diagnosis.

view.note: One finding on the board. The goal is legible, the single result is legible, and there is nothing yet to decide about what to keep.

steps.title: Iteration 5 — working perfectly, already sliding
narrative: Four more states: TX, GA, NY, CA. Four more 2,700-token dumps appended verbatim. The window is 15,860 tokens and the answers are all still correct — the run has not failed, and that is the trap.

What has changed is legibility. Florida's result is now the oldest of five raw blocks, sitting in the middle third of the context, surrounded by four other blocks of near-identical filing text. The fact that Florida was covered is in there. It is just no longer distinguishable from everything else in there.
And notice what the agent is paying for. Each iteration re-sends every previous dump, so by iteration 5 the run has already spent 52,300 input tokens to learn five numbers that fit on one line.
steps.claudeSays: Every prior tool result is still in my context, verbatim. I am re-reading four filing dumps I already summarized in order to make the fifth call.

view.note: Florida's finding — one line — is somewhere inside 2,700 tokens of filing text, now buried under four more blocks that look exactly like it. Nothing is wrong yet. Everything that will go wrong is already set up.

steps.title: Iteration 14 — the rescue that eats the record
narrative: At iteration 14 the append-only window would hit 40,160 tokens and cross the loop's working budget. Auto-compaction (M12) does the responsible thing: it folds iterations 1-9 — 24,300 tokens of raw dumps — into a 600-token summary and drops the originals. The window falls to 16,460 and the run continues.

Read the summary it produced: "Surveyed several southern and eastern states; multiple active liens found; no terminated filings of note." It is fluent, it is broadly true, and it does not contain the word Florida or the number five.

So at iteration 17 the agent, working from a plan that says every state it operates in and a history that no longer names Florida, queries Florida again. It adds those five liens a second time. The run finishes cleanly, reports 41 active liens, and the real number is 36. No exception was raised at any point.
steps.claudeSays: I did not lose the goal. I lost the evidence that I had already satisfied part of it, and re-satisfying it is indistinguishable from making progress.
steps.youDo: Grep your own compaction summaries for the identifiers your loop keys on. Anything the summary cannot name, the loop can do twice.

after.title: AFTER — folded, and Florida is gone

views.text: The compaction did its job: the window is bounded again and the goal is still pinned. What it could not know is that FL was not prose, it was state — the loop's record of work completed. Compressing a summary is safe; compressing a ledger is not.

steps.title: What should have persisted
narrative: The managed loop carries four things across iterations and nothing else: the goal (pinned, never compacted), a done set of states already covered, a running total, and one shaped line per finding — FL: 5 active liens, twenty-two tokens instead of two thousand seven hundred. The raw dump is read, reduced, and dropped in the same step.

Two consequences follow immediately. The done set makes the iteration-17 duplicate impossible — if raw['state'] in self.done: return is the whole guard, and it is a set membership test rather than an act of recall. And the window never exceeds 2,890 tokens at iteration 20, so no compaction ever fires and nothing is ever folded away.

Serialize that state after every iteration and you get the third property for free: a crash at iteration 18 resumes at 19 instead of restarting at 1. Across the run: 448,300 input tokens and a wrong answer, against 53,600 and the right one — 8.4x cheaper, and the cheapness is not the reason to do it.
steps.claudeSays: Each iteration I see the goal, the twelve states I have covered, the running total, and one line per finding. There is nothing in my window to get lost in.
steps.youDo: Give your loop an explicit state object with a done set and a window() method, and make the raw tool result a local variable that goes out of scope.

terminal.text: state.record(raw)   # shape -> append finding -> update total -> drop raw

GOAL: total active lien exposure for ACME + affiliates, all states
DONE: [AL, CA, FL, GA, NC, NY, SC, TX, VA, ...]
FINDINGS: FL: 5 active liens | TX: 4 | GA: 3 | NY: 2 | CA: 6 | ...
RUNNING TOTAL: 36
search_filings(..., state="FL")   # iter 17, retried
FL already in done set — skipped, no call made, no double count
save(state.checkpoint())   # after every iteration

views.text: The append-only loop was never broken. It answered every tool call correctly and finished without an error. It just carried its evidence in a form that a routine, well-intentioned compression could destroy — which is why the discipline is deciding what persists before the pressure arrives, not what to compress once it has.
